I recently made an effort to put a formalization of the P vs NP conjecture in the Deepmind formal-conjectures repository. In the course of that, I did a short formalization of the relevant complexity classes.

It's nice for formal-conjectures to have a famous conjecture like this, but ultimately, I think it would be better if the development of complexity theory could happen in CSLib, for a few reasons

  • It would be nice to develop other classes (PSPACE, EXP, the Polynomial Hierarchy, various probabilistic classes), which would start to balloon the portion of formal-conjectures this would take up.
  • Rather than just stating open questions, it would be nice to actually prove known relationships between these classes. (In particular, to validate that there's nothing wrong with the definitions).
  • Based on the name, I feel like I would be more likely to expect CSLib to have these concepts than Mathlib or formal-conjectures.

So, does this seem like the sort of thing that would make sense to put in CSLib? I know there is a plan for CSLib to have its own language, so perhaps a Turing-machine based formulation of complexity classes doesn't belong for that reason, but I'd be interested in the opinion of anyone who's more actively involved.
There is a way to formalise complexity theory in a word ram model and Emanuelle Viola is writing such a book. Nevertheless it can’t hurt to have the TM version of these classes either.

i think in order to be able to pratically construct reductions for all of the problems in the NP complete class, we need a way of constructing quoted functions in very natural way. Like some sort of embedding of simply typed lambda caluculus and the corresponding formalization of complexity theory for it

that way when you do correctness proof you can interpret the embedded lambda function as a normal lean function and use all of the monadic verification tools to verify the correctness about the reduction program

I know there is a plan for CSLib to have its own language, so perhaps a
Turing-machine based formulation of complexity classes doesn't belong for
that reason

Just curious, what are the advantages of this language over Lean?

For reference, the language is "Boole", you can search Zulip for it, I think the idea is that it will be a procedural language and that it will be easier to reason about time complexity in an embedded DSL rather than native Lean, where it is unclear how we would count the number of steps a function takes to execute.
i think if the language is defined as a type that doesnt contain ani Pi or functions types you define the complexity by interpretting the recursors in some sort of execution model
and then there would prbably be some composition rules for computational complexity

Hey! Sorry I am new to Zulip and am probably putting this in the wrong spot :D

I am a postdoc in Algorithmic Graph Theory and my background is in Computational Geometry. Some friends of mine and I wanted to work on building out some complexity theory tools in lean to hopefully get more people in theory A to formalize their proofs, and we are trying to figure out where to start. One question we had was what is the relationship of ComplexityLib to cslib? I see some overlapping contributors, but it is unclear to me if it is planned on being merged into cslib/mathlib or if its just a fun project/proof of concept?
Are you talking about this complexitylib? https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/complexitylib

If yes, then @Samuel Schlesinger is probably the right person to ask, but if I understand it correctly, complexitylib has a higher amount of AI usage and a lower bar for review / quality control. The benefit is of course that it is much easier to experiment. So in the end I think it would be good to merge it into Cslib in some way or the other, but probably not in its current form.
Ah yeah I realize that message was unclear, but that was the library I meant. Thank you that really helps to clarify things!

Yes, Christian is basically right. Most of us assume that we'll be able to make most of the proofs in there much cleaner and smaller, perhaps by changing the underlying abstractions substantially to something like Christian's RTMs. I started it before CSLib had Multi-Tape TMs, so a major outstanding project for me is refactoring ComplexityLib to rely upon CSLib's Multi-Tape TMs.

If you want to formalize things with Turing Machines and circuits, it is the case that complexitylib is currently in much better shape for doing that than CSLib, it has many more utilities for such things. For context, it is ~10x the size of CSLib at the moment, though it certainly doesn't have close to 10x the size of mathematical content as TM proofs are just enormous in many cases.

Long term, it would be ideal if CSLib grew large enough and capable enough that I don't even maintain anything like complexitylib, but for now it is a testbed for how far I can get in formalizing complexity theory. I am quite confident in much of the underlying formalization despite its larger AI usage, it is the proof quality I am less confident in. I don't think (m)any of the proofs are cheating in any particularly notable ways.

Thank you both for super quick responses! For my applications I would be most interested in building out a catalog of NP-hard problems (subset-sum, vertex cover, other SAT variations) to make it easier to formalize reductions in papers I am writing. Does it make sense to work on this within the framework of complexityLib as it stands given future planned changes? Or should I hold off/work on building up a separate library with less AI code?

I'd recommend joining the efforts of developing complexity for CSLib, this is where the serious development of complexity is going to take place long term with experts like @Christian Reitwiessner.

By the same token, if you end up wanting to contribute to complexitylib and use the tools in there while things are still young in CSLib, feel free. I have Cook-Levin so I'd really like to have a catalogue like that.

This discussion definitely motivates me more than before to port everything in complexitylib to be built atop CSLib.
Great! Thank you so much! We're working through some plans on our end (somehow academic summers are busier than the semester sometimes) but hopefully will seeing you around :)

Hello, everyone! Wouter Swierstra recently wrote a paper on lightweight formal algorithmic complexity.
This August I attended UU's lean summer school and tried to translate the approach to Lean.

My main goal was to use metaprogramming to automate a lot of the work, but my teachers told me that'd be too difficult. Instead I translated the whole paper.
I let an AI work on figuring out the automation.
It says it's correct and it seems correct, but I haven't really checked it.
I presume if this were to be taken up by cslib, one would want to rewrite that part.

I wanted to put this here in case you are interested in exploring easier ways of handling algcom for FP algorithms. ^_^
You can find my work here: https://github.com/nomadalgia/algcomp/tree/main/UuSummerschool2026/Projects/AlgComp
Interesting. This paper post dates my repo which we presented at a STOC workshop this year.
Wouter has been working on this paper for some time. Actually some of my work in the repo is from a previous version (the tree invariant section).

I am not saying that's the only occurrence of the idea of course. Just my inspiration. And then Tanner implemented Freer monads and suggested replacing combinators with FreeM
